We have seen multiple examples of why granting the Meta Muse app "Full Disk Access" on Mac is a terrible idea, and now another major privacy concern has been exposed: Muse has been found to analyze your communications with everyone in your life on an hourly basis.

It's reasonable for Apple to be concerned about this development; the company says in a blog post that it will be introducing extra controls for the Full Disk Access feature—which is at the root of the current issue.

Meta's Muse app has made this urgent

Meta recently rolled out the personal AI assistant Muse for iPhone and Mac. While granting Meta's app full access to all your Apple devices is obviously not something to be encouraged, the app still quickly rose to the top of the App Store charts.

Predictably, things quickly went badly wrong, and there's still no improvement—*Wired* reports that security researcher Karan Joshi discovered that Meta has instructed Muse to gather all the data needed to build a complete map of all your relationships.

One of Muse's instructions appears to give it the ability to "create profile pages for every person in the user's life." The hourly process involves gathering data on family members, partners, friends, colleagues, "collaborators," and people you "follow," with the instructions stating: "where they live, what they do for work, what topics they often discuss (moving, joint savings goals)." It also says the model can note "important dates" such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's history log might include contextual notes such as "a trip in March, a resolved argument, a milestone from last week."

Apple tightens Full Disk Access

You might think the prompt requesting Full Disk Access on Mac is clear enough, but evidently that isn't the case. Even savvy users have granted this broad permission without fully realizing how dangerous it is.

Apple says the feature was originally designed for backup apps, but developers subsequently used it for broader purposes, including AI assistants. The company says it intends to "introduce additional controls" to ensure users fully understand what they're doing when granting this permission.

What Apple must and should do

Apple describes this step as "critical," and I couldn't agree more. When existing permission requests clearly fail to adequately convey the seriousness of granting this access, Apple must ensure users truly understand what they're allowing.

I'd love to see clearer, more explicit wording warning people not to do this unless they're sure of the consequences. For example, something like this:

Basically, the wording can't be too harsh. I'd also welcome a one-time confirmation for apps that have already been granted this permission.

Peter—most-liked comment

While I occasionally find it annoying that Apple asks me if I still want to grant an app access to my location, I do appreciate the design. There have been times when I realized I no longer wanted an app to have that level of access. It also reminds me to periodically think about which apps might be using my location data.

However, Apple absolutely must not repeat what it did with the screen recording feature in macOS Sequoia. The practice itself is dangerous in its own right, and issuing a stern warning is certainly appropriate, but what Apple did at the time was force us to confirm these permissions weekly and every time we restarted the computer.

The practice was widely criticized as turning macOS into Microsoft Vista and imposing "a subscription you didn't buy and can't cancel." In my view, the occasional repeated permission requests on iPhone are already too much. For example, I've already granted Citymapper access to my location so it can provide navigation in the background; Apple, I really don't need you asking me again if I still want to do that.

For granting high-level access, there absolutely should be the strongest possible warning, but if someone chooses to do so, macOS must respect their decision. Thanks, but please don't force weekly or other periodic confirmations.
